name: Silla
summary: One of the Three Kingdoms of Korea and one of its longest-lasting states. Allied with Tang China, it unified most of the peninsula in 668–676 and ruled from Gyeongju.

location.value: Southern and central Korean Peninsula; after 676 most of Korea.

terrain.value: Mountains and river basins in the south-east.

climate.value: Temperate, with hot, wet summers and cold winters.

resources.value: Farmland, gold (famous gold crowns) and iron.

disasters.value: Unknown in detail; chronicles record droughts, famines and earthquakes.

urbanisation.value: Gyeongju was one of the largest cities in East Asia.

migration.value: Absorbed many Goguryeo and Baekje people after unifying Korea.

economicBase.value: Rice farming, with land granted to officials.

tradeRoutes.value: Sea trade with Tang China and Japan; Silla merchants such as Jang Bogo controlled the Yellow Sea in the 9th century.

wealth.value: No estimate is possible; the capital Gyeongju was very rich.

moneyAndTax.value: Taxes in grain, cloth and labour.

inequality.value: The bone-rank system fixed status by birth.

succession.value: Ruled first by the Park, Seok and Kim clans in turn, later by the Kim clan.

institutions.value: The bone-rank system (golpum) fixed people’s status by birth; the Hwarang youth corps trained leaders.

stability.value: Civil wars between nobles in the 9th century weakened the kingdom.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalries between aristocrats over the throne, with about 20 kings in 150 years.

armyAndTech.value: The Hwarang warriors and a large army; crossbows.

majorWars.value: Allied with Tang to conquer Baekje (660) and Goguryeo (668).

territoryChange.value: Unified most of the Korean Peninsula by 676 after defeating Baekje, Goguryeo and Tang forces.

alliancesRivals.value: Allied with Tang China to defeat Baekje (660) and Goguryeo (668), then drove the Tang out.

inventions.value: The Cheomseongdae observatory (7th century), one of the oldest in East Asia.

openness.value: Adopted Buddhism (527) and Tang laws and institutions.

communicationTransport.value: Roads and post stations; sea trade with Tang China and Japan.

religion.value: Buddhism became the state religion; native shamanism continued.

languageWriting.value: Old Korean, written with Chinese characters and the idu system.

artsArchitecture.value: Bulguksa temple and the Seokguram grotto (World Heritage Sites), gold crowns.

sharedIdentity.value: Unification laid the foundations of a single Korean identity.

dailyLife.value: Tiled-roof houses for nobles in Gyeongju, thatched houses for commoners; rice, barley and fish; ondol heated floors in some homes.

neighbours.value: Tang China, Japan and Balhae to the north.

ideasReligions.value: Monks such as Wonhyo and Uisang shaped Korean Buddhism.

riseSignals.value: Founded in 57 BCE by tradition; grew strong after adopting Buddhism (528) and Chinese-style law.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Silla (checked 6 Nov 2026); Seth, A History of Korea (2010)

peakPeriod.value: The 8th century, after unifying most of the peninsula, when Bulguksa and Seokguram were built.

declineSignals.value: Civil wars among aristocrats and rebellions in the 9th century.

outcome.value: The last king surrendered peacefully to Goryeo in 935.

overallCertainty.value: Medium. Early dates are traditional; later history is well recorded.
